title: Ardas at day's end
hookLine: many families close Rehras standing together in Ardas

lines: THIS IS THE PART WHERE WE STAND.
cards: A front room in the evening. The last line of Rehras has been said. A grandmother puts her hands together and gets up from the sofa, a little slowly.
The teenager looks up from her phone, sighs, and stands too. Somebody turns the TV off. The youngest boy stands on the cushion so he's taller.
Nobody announces it. Everyone just knows: this is the part where we stand.

teach.b: Ardas is the Sikh standing prayer. Tradition traces the word to a Persian phrase for a petition, the kind of written request a subject would bring to a ruler.
Sikhs say it standing, hands folded, often facing the Guru Granth Sahib if one is in the house. One person leads; the others listen, and say Waheguru together at certain points.

It isn't a shabad from the Guru Granth Sahib. It's the community's own prayer, with a standard form set out in the Sikh code of conduct. It opens by remembering: the ten Gurus by name, then the Guru Granth Sahib.

teach.h: REMEMBER: THE GURUS, THE SIKHS WHO KEPT FAITH.
teach.b: Then the long line of Sikhs who kept faith, who served, who suffered and gave their lives, are brought to mind. Then comes the asking, for the whole community and for the world.
And there's a place where a family can name tonight's particular reason: a grandfather in hospital, a new baby, an exam tomorrow, a safe journey.

teach.h: SARBAT DAA BHALAA: MAY ALL BE WELL.
teach.b: Then the close, in its set words: Nanak naam chardhi kalaa, tere bhaane sarbat daa bhalaa. In paraphrase: through Nanak's Name, may spirits rise; by Your will, may all be well. Not may we be well.

May all be well. So the family in the front room ends the day by standing up for everyone, and naming the one or two people on their mind. Then the Sikh greeting: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh.

how: Sikh families often stand together for Ardas after Rehras, hands folded, one person leading and all saying Waheguru at set points; it ends with Nanak naam chardhi kalaa, tere bhaane sarbat daa bhalaa.

o: a hymn from the Guru Granth Sahib, sung
a standing prayer, a petition to the One
a sermon given by the gurdwara's leader

s: Ardas is a shabad from the Guru Granth Sahib
it's the community's prayer, with a standard form in the Sikh code of conduct.
Ardas ends by asking for the good of all
tere bhaane sarbat daa bhalaa: by Your will, may all be well.
a family can name a particular need in Ardas
a sick grandparent, a new baby, a journey.

games.q: the family stands for Ardas at day's end. how does the prayer close?
o: asking that this family be blessed above others.
asking that by the Lord's will all be well.
games.why: Nanak naam chardhi kalaa, tere bhaane sarbat daa bhalaa: not may we be well, but may all be well.

practice: Stand if you can, feet steady and hands together, or sit up straight, and bring to mind the people who carried you here: parents, teachers, anyone who kept faith before you.
Name one person on your mind tonight; if you pray, hold them before God in the plain words of your heart, or say Waheguru. Then widen it, the way Ardas does: may all be well.

wordCard.voice: Ardas, the Sikh standing prayer that closes Rehras in many homes: remembering the Gurus and the faithful, naming tonight's need, and asking that all be well.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: ardaas, the Sikh standing prayer, a petition.

carryVoice: Your line: stand at day's end. Not may we be well; may all be well. That's day four hundred seventeen.
